newsitem.title: UK: Toxic cadmium found in British sheep - magazine.
newsitem.headline: Toxic cadmium found in British sheep - magazine.

text.p: British sheep that graze on land fertilised with sewer sludge have accumulated high levels of poisonous cadmium in their livers and kidneys, New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
It said British scientists would announce the findings, preliminary results of a study commissioned by the agriculture ministry, at a British Society of Animal Science conference next week.

Mike Wilkinson, of consultants Chalcombe Agricultural Resources in Lincoln, working with Julian Hill, of Writtle College in Chelmsford, compared levels of heavy metals accumulated by sheep grazing on a field treated with sludge and another that was untreated.
After five months average levels of cadmium in the livers of the animals grazing on the treated pasture was eight times higher than in the other sheep. Levels in the kidneys were six times higher.

"If the practice of spreading sewage sludge on pasture intensifies, as is likely in Europe after 1998 when dumping at sea is banned, people who eat lambs' livers or kidneys regularly might be at risk of chronic cadmium poisoning," New Scientist quoted the report as saying.
The magazine said it was not clear if there was enough cadmium in the sheep's organs to exceed World Health Organisation daily intake limits of 70 micrograms for people.
The ministry of agriculture said people would consume less than the WHO limit "even if they ate the meat with the observed levels for the rest of their lives".

In the mid 1950s thousands of people in Japan's Fuchu region suffered painful bone and kidney disorders after eating as much as two milligrams of cadmium a day in rice irrigated with contaminated water.
